label: bm-architecture-gaps
topic: Unmet needs in bio-based and responsive architectural materials, deeply sourced
summary: Across mycelium, bioplastics (PLA, PHA), engineered timber, bacterial cellulose, algae, chitosan, living building materials and passive responsive skins, the sourced picture is: only timber is mature and standardised; mycelium is commercial for insulation/packaging (TRL 7-9) but research-stage (TRL 3-5) for anything structural, with no verified reaction-to-fire classification (full-scale EN 13501-1 'rarely used', one EI 15 resistance test; the only 'Euroclass B' is a company statement); PLA is cheap (2-3 USD/kg) but its glass transition is 55-80 C and pure printed PLA fell from about 28 MPa to below 10 MPa in 12 weeks of simulated UV; PHA costs 3-8 USD/kg (algal PHA 7-9); bacterial cellulose has a 15-138 GPa fibre modulus on paper but bulk sheets are 180 MPa dry and 3 MPa wet (a 58x swing), costs 70-270 EUR/kg dry at lab scale and is 'in its infancy of commercialization'; algae facades are pump-and-glass photobioreactors, not materials; chitosan composites have a cost (about 2 USD/kg) but no durability data; living building materials die on drying, while a non-living microalgae bio-cement did earn ASTM C90/C129 certification in 2023. For passive responsive skins the best system (Freiburg, 424 cellulose bilayer modules) reports shade coverage only: its authors say quantifying indoor-climate benefit is future work and 170 cycles is small against a building life. I confirm the earlier record on Elastic 50A (39.2 percent IPA, 24 h) and Rigid 10K (<0.1 percent), and CORRECT one earlier claim: spec-resin-chemistry said every current SLA resin gains under 1 percent in water, but Formlabs' Flexible 80A V2 datasheet (ASTM D471, parsed by word coordinates) shows +8 percent mass and +3 percent volume after 1 day in deionized water (+9 and +7 percent after 1 week). With a non-swelling partner and the project's 3/2 ceiling this gives, by my own arithmetic, a bending radius of about 67 mm at 1 mm thickness after 1 day of immersion (isotropic-strain assumption; immersion, not humid air). Ranked gaps for a small computation-heavy team with a desktop printer: (1) humid-air swelling constants and response times for printable materials, (2) a measured/simulated link from responsive-skin geometry to solar gain and daylight, (3) a cycling-plus-UV durability protocol for printed responsive parts, (4) transparent embodied-carbon and provenance accounting for the proof of concept (only 18 percent of emerging structural materials have an embodied-carbon value), (5) printed load-bearing/drainage scaffolds for weak, wet bio-fills. Fire certification, living materials and bacterial-cellulose structure are not addressable by this team.
lay_summary: Most 'green' building materials are still not ready to hold up a building. Timber is the exception: it has rulebooks and a market price. Mushroom-based panels work as insulation, but nobody has published a proper fire-class test for them, and bacterial cellulose is very strong as a single thread yet turns soft like a wet jelly when it takes up water. The best 'self-moving' facade so far, in Freiburg, opens and closes with the weather using no power, but its builders only measured how much shade it gave, not how much energy it saves. For our small team the cheapest honest wins are measurement jobs: record how fast and how far printed strips curl as the air gets damper, test them for thousands of cycles, and put an honest carbon number on the printed samples. A bendy strip made of two layers, one that swells in moisture and one that does not, is like a wet-then-dry paper strip curling on a table.

glossary.plain: A 1 to 9 scale: 1 is an idea, 9 is a product proven in real use.
Two bonded layers where one swells with moisture and the other does not, so the strip bends when the air gets damper.
A foam-like material grown from fungal threads through farm waste, then dried.
A mat of very fine cellulose fibres made by bacteria in a tray of sugar liquid.
Two plastics made from plant sugar (PLA) or bacteria (PHA), which can break down under the right conditions.
Wooden boards glued in crossing layers to make large structural panels.
A sliding failure across the wood grain inside the crossed layers of CLT.
The European labels (A1 to F) for how easily a building product burns.
A wall or panel kept flames out (E) and heat down (I) for 15 minutes in a fire-resistance test.
A glass or plastic tank of water and algae that needs pumps, light and air.
The greenhouse gas released making a material, before it is ever used.
How stiff a material is: the force needed to stretch it a given amount.
How tightly a strip bends; a smaller radius means a tighter curl.
Soaking a sample fully in liquid, which is harsher than damp air.
The temperature where a plastic goes from hard to soft and starts to sag under load.
Slow, permanent sagging of a material under a steady load.
US standards for load-bearing and non-load-bearing concrete masonry blocks.
A small-sample fire test that measures how much heat a burning material gives off.

findings.claim: Mycelium-bound composite research mostly sits at TRL 3-5, while packaging and insulation applications reach TRL 7-9.
findings.evidence_quote: Most MBC research currently resides between TRL 3 and TRL 5, where laboratory validation and early prototyping dominate

findings.claim: A 2026 quantitative synthesis reports mycelium compressive strength of 0.05-1.2 MPa, narrower than the 0.03-4.44 MPa range in the 2025 review used in the earlier file; both are reported, they come from different review sets.
findings.evidence_quote: A comparative synthesis of reported data reveals significant variability in compressive strength (0.05-1.2 MPa) and elastic modulus

findings.claim: Full-scale EN 13501-1 reaction-to-fire testing is rarely done for mycelium composites; the cited exception tested mycelium-Miscanthus panels for fire resistance (not reaction-to-fire class) and reached EI 15. This confirms and strengthens the earlier 'no fire classification' gap.
findings.evidence_quote: Full-scale testing in accordance with the BS EN 13501-1 standard [25] is rarely used for MBCs owing to its high cost, complexity, and large sample size.

findings.claim: The only Euroclass figure for a mycelium insulation I found is a company statement on an accelerator profile (Mykor: Euroclass B, REI 60-120); no test report was seen. A search summary also mentioned a Euroclass E for another product, which I could not verify and do not use.
findings.evidence_quote: with greater fire performance rating of Euroclass B and resistance REI of 60-120

findings.claim: Mycelium panel production cost is quoted by a review as about 0.83 USD per cubic foot (secondary estimate); converted by me to 29.3 USD/m3.
findings.evidence_quote: Mycelium panel production is estimated at $0.83 per cubic foot

findings.claim: The 2025 review names low strength, weathering susceptibility, scalability, under-50-year life and lack of standard test methods as barriers for mycelium (confirms the earlier file).
findings.evidence_quote: including low mechanical strength, weathering susceptibility, scalability issues, limited lifespan (<50 years), and a lack of standardised manufacturing/testing methods

findings.claim: PLA property ranges and price in the Nature Communications 2026 comparison table: Tg 55-80 C, modulus 0.3-3.8 GPa, tensile 10-80 MPa, price 2-3 USD/kg.
findings.evidence_quote: PLA Chemical industrial synthesis 6–9 weeks >1.5 years 55–80 0.3–3.8 10–80 NA 37 80% 2–3

findings.claim: PHA property ranges and price in the same table: Tg -10 to 15 C, modulus 0.4-3.8 GPa, tensile 15-45 MPa, price 3-8 USD/kg. Column mapping is mine from the table header.
findings.evidence_quote: PHA Bacterial extraction 1–4 months 1–6 months -10−15 0.4–3.8 15–45 NA 55–72 47.8% 3–8

findings.claim: A techno-economic study cited by an algal-bioplastic review puts algal PHA at 7-9 USD/kg, uncompetitive with petroleum plastic.
findings.evidence_quote: estimated PHA production cost between $7 and to 9 per kg, which is still uncompetitive compared to petroleum-derived plastic

findings.claim: Printed pure PLA lost most of its strength in 12 weeks of simulated UV: about 28 MPa initially and below 10 MPa after 12 weeks (coupon FDM test, laboratory lamp, not outdoor). A 10 percent coffee-ground filler kept 24-25 MPa. My retention bound is at most 36 percent (10/28).
findings.evidence_quote: after 12 weeks of UV degradation, there is a significant reduction in strength to below 10 MPa, indicating significant disruption of the polymer chain due to photo-degradation

findings.claim: Lab creep studies of printed PLA exist (ASTM D2990 coupons, desktop FDM printer) but I found none at facade temperature and humidity, so a building creep number for PLA remains unverified (absence of evidence from this search only).
findings.evidence_quote: The geometry of creep test specimens follows the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM D2990) standards.

findings.claim: North American CLT market price has been steady at about 42-44 USD per cubic foot over two years, which I convert to 1483-1554 USD/m3 (35.315 ft3 per m3); for an assumed 100 mm panel that is 148-155 USD/m2 (assumption, not from the source).
findings.evidence_quote: Prices have held fairly steady during the last 2 years at around $42 to $44 dollars

findings.claim: A 2019 techno-economic model gives CLT mill-gate minimum selling prices of 536 USD/m3 (large plant) and 652 USD/m3 (small plant), versus 600-742 USD/m3 literature values.
findings.evidence_quote: has a minimum selling price of $536/m3.

findings.claim: CLT is covered by EN 16351:2021 and ANSI/APA PRG 320-2019; weak rolling shear is the cited limit for large-span heavy-load use.
findings.evidence_quote: the weak transverse layer rolling shear performance limits the application of CLT in large-span heavy-load structures

findings.claim: Embodied-carbon data are missing for most emerging structural materials; engineered wood and reused steel reach 3-5 percent of primary steel's cradle-to-gate EC in the authors' beam case (stored carbon excluded).
findings.evidence_quote: Only 18% (37 out of 204) of the emerging structural materials reviewed had EC values; less (11%) had embodied energy values.

findings.claim: Bacterial cellulose fibres/ideal material are reported at 15-138 GPa modulus, 60-90 percent crystallinity.
findings.evidence_quote: BC has a crystallinity of up to 60% to 90% and a young’s modulus of up to 15 to 138 Gpa

findings.claim: Measured bulk BC sheets are far weaker than the fibre figure: crude dry BC 180.3 MPa modulus, 11.6 MPa strength; crude fresh hydrated BC 3.1 MPa modulus, 1.2 MPa strength (a 58x drop, my ratio 180.3/3.1). This is a biomedical-materials study, not an architectural element.
Lab-scale BC production cost fell from 0.25-0.27 to 0.07-0.08 EUR per g with flour-based nitrogen substitution, i.e. 70-270 EUR/kg dry.
findings.evidence_quote: the maximum reduction was observed for BY-BC at 50% substitution (from 0.25 to 0.07 €/g; 72.00%)

findings.claim: BC bioplastic commercialisation is described as just beginning and held back by cost.
findings.evidence_quote: BC’s adoption as a biodegradable bioplastic is still in its infancy of commercialization, primarily constrained by high production costs.

findings.claim: The architecture-specific BC literature I found is conceptual: a 2021 paper proposes BC as structural and membrane material and says mechanical enhancement for structural use is ongoing; the abstract gives no strength or durability numbers.
findings.evidence_quote: the current study is part of the ongoing research on enhancing the mechanical properties of bacterial cellulose in order to use it for structural applications

findings.claim: Algae facades are pumped glass-panel photobioreactor systems; the BIQ house has 129 flat-panel glass PBRs and is called very complex, and in an LCA of a column PBR cultivation electricity caused almost all CO2.
findings.evidence_quote: BIQ house is very complex, consisting of 129 flat panel glass PBRs, making even the cleaning and maintenance cost higher than in this study.

findings.claim: A microalgae-derived bio-cement block received ASTM C129 and C90 certification in February 2023 (company press coverage); it is non-living, so it refines the earlier view that bio-based mineral materials are lab-only.
findings.evidence_quote: Prometheus Materials has been awarded ASTM C129 certification for non-loadbearing concrete masonry units (CMU) and ASTM C90 for loadbearing CMUs for its bio-cement product.

findings.claim: Among microbial mineralisation (MICP) uses, self-healing concrete is the most commercially mature and geotechnical uses are TRL 5-7; the review lists long-term durability data, scale-specific cost and monitoring protocols as gaps.
findings.evidence_quote: The self healing concrete application is the most advanced toward commercial maturity, and there are products available from Basilisk, Evonik and BioMason.

findings.claim: Chitosan-cellulose FLAM costs about 2 USD/kg with 0.26 GPa modulus; at high chitosan content the composite shrinks during drying and loses integrity. I found no moisture, weathering or outdoor-durability data in the paper text (confirms the earlier file).
findings.evidence_quote: high amounts of chitosan (>17%) produce strong internal forces as the polymers loses water and shrinks, undermining the integrity of structure

findings.claim: The Freiburg 4D-printed cellulose shading evaluated shade coverage only; the authors say quantifying indoor-climate improvement is future work (no energy or comfort number exists for it).
findings.evidence_quote: While we have focused on evaluating the 4D-printed shading elements through analysis of shade coverage in this study, it will be important to quantify the improvement of indoor climate regulation in future work.

findings.claim: Only 170 actuation cycles were tested, which the authors call small against a building's lifetime; UV exposure marginally lowered curvature at low RH.
findings.evidence_quote: The number of cycles tested is still small compared to the entire lifetime of a building

findings.claim: Freiburg manufacturing figures: 18.25 printer-hours per m2 of facade, 5.5 kg actuating and 0.7 kg restricting filament in total (0.59 and 0.07 kg/m2), cellulose powder at 1.52 EUR/kg; implied area 5.5/0.59 = 9.3 m2.
findings.evidence_quote: Using four 3D-printers (working 10 hours per day), the rate of 4D-printing manufacturing is 18.25 hm −2

findings.claim: Only 10.3 percent of studies in a 2026 systematic map of biomimetic interior-comfort strategies report statistically validated findings and half are review- or concept-led (interior comfort field, not facades; used as an indicator of weak evidence stratification).
findings.evidence_quote: only 10.3% of studies report statistically validated empirical findings, whereas 50.0% remain review-based or concept-led.

findings.claim: CORRECTION of spec-resin-chemistry.json ('every current SLA resin gains under 1% mass in water ... Flexible 80A 0.7%'): the Flexible 80A V2 datasheet shows +8 percent mass and +3 percent volume after 1 day in deionized water and +9 and +7 percent after 1 week (ASTM D471 slabs). The 0.7 percent row is the older 'Flexible 80A Resin' in the 1 cm cube table; there is no V2 row there. spec-formlabs-materials.json had this right.
findings.evidence_quote: Deionized Water 1 day -26 +8% +3% 94% 89%

findings.claim: Using the project's 3/2 ceiling and isotropic linear strain from the 3 percent volume change (0.99 percent), a Flexible 80A V2 layer bonded to a non-swelling layer would bend to a radius of about 67 mm at 1 mm total thickness after one day of immersion (11.7-134.7 mm over the cases in the table). Immersion, not humid air; swelling would need to be re-measured in air.

Reconfirmed from Formlabs' 24 h table: Elastic 50A V2 gains 39.2 percent in isopropyl alcohol and 0.7 percent in water; Rigid 10K gains under 0.1 percent in both. This confirms the earlier 39 percent versus under 0.1 percent claim (and the warning that 163.9 is the xylene column).
findings.evidence_quote: Results are reported as weight gain percentage after 24 hours of exposure to solvent.

findings.claim: DISAGREEMENT on polyamide moisture strain: the earlier file estimated 0.2-0.45 percent hygroscopic strain for PA12 (from mass uptake, calibrated on PA6.6); a 2021 hot-pressed PA11/PA12 durability paper states water or moisture causes no hardness or dimension change. I could not find dimension data in its text, and it is hot-pressed sheet, not sintered. Neither is a measurement on Fuse powders.
findings.evidence_quote: absorbed water or moisture does not cause plasticization; thus, neither hardness nor dimension changes.

findings.claim: Waste-based bioplastic wall-cladding tiles were tested for acoustics, mechanics and heat but only for non-load-bearing interior use; the authors list long-term durability and fire resistance as future work.
findings.evidence_quote: Future research directions include evaluating long-term durability, fire resistance, and advanced formulations to expand the applications of bioplastic cladding in modern architecture.

findings.claim: Independent numerical re-check of the project record: the Timoshenko coefficient f(m,n) peaks at exactly 1.5 at m = n^(-1/2) for n = 0.1, 1, 2, 5, 10, 50 (grid maximum 1.5 in each case), and equal layers at n=10 give f = 0.9959, a 33.6 percent loss. The earlier file rounded this to 34 percent.

key_claims.claim: The best passive bio-based skin has no building-performance number and a short durability record, so the open gap is the link from actuator geometry to measured or simulated solar gain and cycle life.
key_claims.evidence_quote: While we have focused on evaluating the 4D-printed shading elements through analysis of shade coverage in this study, it will be important to quantify the improvement of indoor climate regulation in future work.

key_claims.claim: Among stock Formlabs SLA resins, Flexible 80A V2 is the one with large water uptake (+8 percent mass, +3 percent volume in 1 day, immersion), which contradicts the earlier blanket 'under 1 percent' statement and is the only catalogue resin with swelling big enough for a hygromorph layer; humid-air constants remain unpublished.

Mycelium and other living or fungal materials lack a verified reaction-to-fire class and are research-stage (TRL 3-5) beyond insulation and packaging, so they are the wrong first target for a small computational team.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Full-scale testing in accordance with the BS EN 13501-1 standard [25] is rarely used for MBCs owing to its high cost, complexity, and large sample size.

key_claims.claim: Embodied-carbon data are missing for most emerging structural materials, so a transparent carbon sheet for the proof of concept is a real, computation-only contribution.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Only 18% (37 out of 204) of the emerging structural materials reviewed had EC values; less (11%) had embodied energy values.

recommendations: Pitch the new biomaterial as a law-constrained printable hygromorph (bilayer with the 3/2 ceiling built in) rather than a mycelium, bacterial-cellulose, algae or living material; those need fire, biosafety or growth infrastructure the team does not have.

Do gap 1 first (humid-air swelling constants and response time for Flexible 80A V2, Silicone 40A, Rigid 10K, Nylon 11 and a hydrogel resin if open mode is licensed); it unlocks gaps 2 and 3 and settles the PA12 disagreement.
Never quote an energy saving, a fire class, or a PLA creep life for the printed demonstrator; report curvature, cycles and modelled shading only, labelled as such.
Quote bacterial-cellulose stiffness only as wet versus dry bulk-sheet numbers (3.1 versus 180 MPa), not the 15-138 GPa fibre figure.

For the practice conversation, offer gap 4 (a carbon and provenance sheet with a script) alongside the physical samples, since the practice's own PLA carbon-saving figures disagree across sources (project record).
Before relying on the Flexible 80A V2 number, re-measure it in humid air and on a printed Form 4 coupon; the TDS slab was wiped wet after immersion and the table was scrambled in text extraction.

could_not_find: Cost per m2 for mycelium panels, bacterial cellulose, algae or chitosan elements: only per-kg, per-m3 or per-gram figures exist; the CLT per-m2 figure is my conversion for an assumed 100 mm panel. The 4D-printed cellulose skin has filament mass and printer-hours per m2 but no published price per m2.

Any independent EN 13501-1 or ASTM E84 test report for a mycelium panel; Mykor's Euroclass B is a company statement and a Euroclass E claim for another product came only from a search summary (Biohm page fetched had no fire text; Mogu page returned 404; Mykor news page returned 403).

A source-stated TRL for bacterial cellulose, algae facades, chitosan or passive skins: the TRL values for those rows are my judgement from the evidence described, labelled as such. Only mycelium and MICP TRLs are source-stated.
Mechanical or durability numbers for bacterial cellulose as a real architectural element (only a conceptual 2021 paper and biomedical-sheet data were found).

Humid-air (RH) swelling coefficient or diffusivity for any Formlabs resin or powder; the PA11/PA12 dimensional-change statement is from a hot-pressed sheet abstract and I did not find the data behind it.
PLA or PHA creep, hydrolysis and weathering numbers at real facade temperature and humidity; PLA UV data are from a laboratory lamp on FDM coupons.
Moisture, weathering and outdoor-durability data for chitosan-cellulose composites; cost and standards for living building materials.

ICC-ES or European Technical Assessment status of any mycelium or microalgae-cement product (EOTA ETA database and ICC-ES reports were not queried); the Prometheus ASTM certification comes from trade-press coverage, not the certificate.
Values read from figures: the Mass Timber Performance Index chart and the Freiburg shade-coverage curves were not read as numbers beyond what the text states.
Measured (not modelled) energy or comfort saving for any power-free bio-based responsive facade: none found, consistent with the earlier file.

Coverage bias: most full texts came through Europe PMC and are open access; Crossref was rate-limited (HTTP 429) on rapid queries so some searches were slower; OpenAlex was not used, per the rules. MDPI/Elsevier paywalled literature on PLA and BC mechanics was therefore mostly unread.
The practice's own statements on UV, creep, moisture and fire were not re-searched; the buyer entries rely on the project-record file spec-partner-architecture.json for the practice's needs.
